title: JESUS EXPLAINED THE BRONZE SERPENT TO NICODEMUS—AND MANY CHRISTIANS READ RIGHT PAST IT
paragraphs:
JESUS EXPLAINED THE BRONZE SERPENT TO NICODEMUS—AND MANY CHRISTIANS READ RIGHT PAST IT
The strange Old Testament story Jesus deliberately brought into a midnight conversation about salvation—and why understanding it may change the way you see the Cross forever.
There was poison in their blood.
People were dying.
And God told Moses to make a serpent.
If that sentence sounds strange, it should.

Because thousands of years later, during one of the most important conversations ever recorded, Jesus reached back into that disturbing scene in the wilderness and told Nicodemus that what happened there was pointing toward Him.
Not merely toward healing.
Not merely toward faith.
Toward the Cross.
And once you understand why Jesus chose this particular story, John 3:16—the verse almost everybody knows—begins to burn with a depth many people have never noticed.
But first, you have to walk into the wilderness.
You have to hear the cries.
You have to see what sin had done.
And perhaps hardest of all...
you have to admit that the dying people in that wilderness may look more like us than we want to believe.
Numbers 21 records Israel becoming impatient during the journey. They spoke against God and against Moses:
“Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?”
They despised the provision God had given them.
Then came judgment.
Numbers 21:6 says:
וַיְשַׁלַּח יְהוָה בָּעָם אֵת הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים
Vayeshallaḥ YHWH ba'am et-hanneḥashim hasśerafim.
The LORD sent among the people the “fiery serpents.”
The Hebrew expression הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (hanneḥashim hasśerafim) combines the word for serpents with a term related to burning. The text does not invite us to romanticize what happened.
People were bitten.
People died.
Then something changed.
The people came to Moses and finally said the words rebellion hates to say:
“We have sinned.”
Not...
“We made mistakes.”
Not...
“We were misunderstood.”
Not...
“Everybody has issues.”
“We have sinned.”
That confession matters.
Because grace becomes cheap whenever sin becomes imaginary.
The people asked Moses to intercede, and God gave him an astonishing command:
“Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.”
So Moses made a bronze serpent and lifted it up.
Imagine being bitten.
The venom is already inside you.
Your strength is disappearing.
You cannot negotiate with the poison.
You cannot outrun it.
You cannot become moral enough to reverse it.
You cannot promise the venom that tomorrow you will do better.
You are dying.
Then comes the word:
Look.
That is all.
Look at what God has provided.
And live.
The Hebrew of Numbers 21:9 says that when a bitten person looked toward the bronze serpent,
וָחָי
vāḥāy.
“And he lived.”
Do not rush past that.
He lived.
Not because bronze possesses healing power.
Not because staring at an object is magic.
Not because Moses invented a religious technique.
God attached His promise to the provision He commanded.
The dying person had nothing with which to boast.
He could only trust the word of God enough to look.
Centuries passed.
The bronze serpent itself eventually became a trap. Israel began burning incense to it, and King Hezekiah destroyed it. Second Kings 18:4 even records the contemptuous name given to it:
נְחֻשְׁתָּן
Nehushtan.
Essentially, a piece of bronze.
Think about the irony.
Something God once used became something people later idolized.
Human beings are remarkably capable of worshiping the instrument while forgetting the God who gave it.
We can do it with traditions.
Buildings.
Leaders.
Platforms.
Denominations.
Religious objects.
Even ministries.
Nothing that points toward Jesus should ever be allowed to replace Jesus.
Then, centuries after Moses raised that serpent in the wilderness, a Pharisee walked through the darkness to speak privately with Christ.
His name was Nicodemus.
John tells us he came to Jesus “by night.”
Nicodemus was not spiritually uneducated.
He was a Pharisee.
A ruler of the Jews.
Jesus later called him “the teacher of Israel.”
This was not an ignorant pagan asking Christianity 101 questions.
This was a religious man.
A knowledgeable man.
A respected man.
And Jesus told him:
“You must be born again.”
Imagine what that must have done to him.
Nicodemus had pedigree.
Jesus spoke of birth.
Nicodemus had religious achievement.
Jesus spoke of something only God could ultimately produce.
Nicodemus had knowledge.
Jesus exposed his need.
The Greek phrase translated “born again” is:
γεννηθῆναι ἄνωθεν
gennēthēnai anōthen.
The word ἄνωθεν (anōthen) can carry the sense of “again” and “from above,” and John appears to exploit that richness. Nicodemus hears Jesus in terms of another physical birth.
Jesus is speaking about the radical life of the Spirit that comes from above.
Nicodemus knew religion.
But religion could not resurrect him.
And that is where some of us need to stop pretending.
You can know worship songs and still need Christ.
You can quote Scripture and still need Christ.
You can attend church and still need Christ.
You can have Christian parents, Christian friends, Christian books, Christian tattoos, Christian posts, Christian vocabulary and a carefully maintained Christian reputation...
and still desperately need Christ.
Jesus did not tell Nicodemus to polish the old man.
He told him he needed new birth.
Then Jesus reached into Israel's Scriptures and chose the story of poisoned people staring at a bronze serpent.
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
The Greek is startling:
καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, οὕτως ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
Kai kathōs Mōysēs hypsōsen ton ophin en tē erēmō, houtōs hypsōthēnai dei ton huion tou anthrōpou.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”
There is one little Greek word here that should stop us:
δεῖ
dei.
“Must.”
The Son of Man must be lifted up.
The Cross was not an unfortunate interruption in Jesus' mission.
The Cross was central to His mission.
Jesus had come to save sinners.

Later in John, the language of Jesus being “lifted up” clearly points toward His death. John 12:32–33 records Jesus saying that when He is lifted up from the earth He will draw people to Himself, and John immediately explains that He said this to indicate the kind of death He would die.
Jesus was going to be lifted up.
Not upon a throne of earthly conquest.
Upon a Roman cross.
But there is a question here that can make the whole passage uncomfortable:
Why compare Himself with the serpent?

The bronze serpent was not evil magic and it was not a portrait suggesting Christ Himself was sinful. Scripture is emphatic that Jesus “knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21), “did no sin” (1 Peter 2:22), and was “without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
Yet Paul gives us language that helps illuminate the scandal of the Cross:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
And Galatians 3:13 declares:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.”
The sinless One stood where the guilty should have stood.
He bore what belonged to us.
Isaiah had already spoken of the Servant who would be “wounded for our transgressions” and “bruised for our iniquities.”
The serpent lifted in the wilderness represented before the dying Israelites the very judgment associated with their condition, while God's appointed provision brought life to those who looked.
At Calvary, something infinitely greater happened.
Jesus did not merely stand near sinners.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree.
The Holy One entered the place of condemnation without becoming sinful Himself.
The Judge stepped into the judgment.
The innocent Son bore the penalty of the guilty.
And suddenly the wilderness does not feel ancient anymore.
Because there is poison in us too.
We just give it respectable names.
Pride becomes “knowing my worth.”
Greed becomes “ambition.”
Lust becomes “just being human.”
Bitterness becomes “protecting my peace.”
Gossip becomes “telling the truth.”
Unforgiveness becomes “having boundaries.”
Self-righteousness becomes “discernment.”
Secret compromise becomes “nobody's perfect.”
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, we learn how to decorate what Jesus came to crucify.
That may be the serpent bite we keep reading past.
The Israelites could see the wounds on their bodies.
Our wounds can hide behind church clothes.
Behind ministry.
Behind Bible verses.
Behind smiles.
But God sees beneath the profile picture.
He knows what happened last night.
He knows the thought you keep feeding.
He knows the person you still hate.
He knows the browser history.
He knows the jealousy.
He knows the secret messages.
He knows the prayerlessness.
He knows the addiction nobody knows exists.
He knows the tears you wipe away before anybody enters the room.
And He knows something else too.
He knows exactly how helpless you are to save yourself.
That is why the Gospel is such offensive news to human pride...
and such beautiful news to exhausted sinners.
The dying Israelite did not heal himself before looking.
He looked because he could not heal himself.
And Christianity does not begin with becoming good enough for Jesus.
It begins with admitting you never could be.
The Gospel does not say:
Fix yourself and perhaps God will love you.
It says that God acted for sinners who could not rescue themselves.
And immediately after Jesus speaks about the serpent being lifted up, John gives us words known around the world:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...”
Do you see the connection now?
John 3:16 was not dropped randomly onto a greeting card.
It comes immediately after Jesus speaks about dying people in the wilderness and the Son of Man being lifted up.
“For God so loved the world...”
This is love standing in the shadow of a cross.
Not sentimental love.
Not indulgent love.
Holy love.
Costly love.
Saving love.
A love that does not pretend the poison is harmless.
A love that provides the remedy at unimaginable cost.
The Greek verb John repeatedly uses for believing is πιστεύω (pisteuō).
Biblical faith is not merely admitting that Jesus existed.
The demons know who He is.
Saving faith looks away from self and rests in Christ.
The Israelites did not stare at their wounds until the wounds healed.
They looked toward God's provision.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years staring at the wound.
“I ruined my marriage.”
“I betrayed somebody.”
“I had the abortion.”
“I cheated.”
“I became addicted.”
“I walked away from God.”
“I wasted years.”
“I knew better.”
“I failed my children.”
“I preached things I wasn't living.”
“I don't even recognize myself anymore.”
You keep staring at the bite.
Jesus says:
Look to Me.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Because Christ bore judgment for everyone who belongs to Him.
Not because repentance does not matter.
True faith turns toward Christ, and Christ does not merely forgive us so that we can comfortably return to the chains He died to break.
Grace is not permission to keep petting the serpent.
Grace calls sinners out of darkness.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
It is the turning of a heart that has stopped defending its rebellion and comes to Christ empty-handed.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
We prefer complicated salvation because complicated salvation leaves room for pride.
Give us ten religious achievements.
Give us fifty prayers.
Give us a mountain to climb.
Give us something impressive enough that when we finally reach heaven, we can quietly believe we helped save ourselves.
But God puts a dying man in the desert and says:
Look.
Then He puts His crucified Son before the world and says:
Believe.
There is no trophy for the poisoned man.
There is only mercy.
And maybe you have been trying to earn what Jesus purchased.
Maybe you have been punishing yourself because accepting forgiveness feels too easy.
But look again at Calvary and tell me grace was easy.
It was free to you.
It was not cheap to Him.
There were nails.
There was blood.
There was shame.
There was rejection.
There was a crown of thorns.
There was darkness.
And there was the sinless Son of God willingly laying down His life.
Then came the tomb.
Then came Sunday.
And the One who was lifted up on the Cross walked out of the grave alive.
Christian hope does not end with a dying Savior.
We proclaim a risen King.
The serpent story therefore forces a question far more personal than theological curiosity:
Where are you looking?
At yourself?
Your morality?
Your church attendance?
Your accomplishments?
Your suffering?
Your failures?
Your religious reputation?
Your pastor?
Your denomination?
Your past?
Or Christ?
Because the bronze serpent itself eventually became an idol.
And Christians can still turn things that should point toward Christ into substitutes for Christ.
Even Gospel Warrior must never become that.
This ministry is not your Savior.
No pastor is your Savior.
No Christian book is your Savior.
No amount of sharing religious content saves your soul.
Jesus Christ saves.
That distinction matters deeply to us.
If this article exposed something you have hidden behind religion, don't manufacture a polished response. Be honest before God.
And believers who see those words...
pray.
Don't perform.
Don't condemn.
Pray.
Because there are real human beings behind those comments.
Somebody may be fighting for their marriage.
Somebody may be trying not to return to an addiction.
Somebody may be sitting alone wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
Somebody may have walked into church smiling this morning and cried in the car afterward.
Somebody needs to discover that Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted His church.
Jesus transformed Paul into an apostle.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to construct an impressive religious résumé.
He had only a dying plea:
“Lord, remember me.”
And Jesus gave him paradise.
That is scandalous grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that is powerful enough to rescue evil people and begin making them new.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
God still knows it.
Maybe your scandal happened entirely inside your heart.
God knows that too.
Maybe everybody applauds the version of you they see while you are terrified of the version only God sees.
Christ already knows.
And still the Cross stands.
Look.
The blood has not lost its power because your story became ugly.
The resurrection did not become less true because you fell again.
But do not confuse grace with permission to remain where grace found you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Seek accountability where needed.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Run from what keeps dragging you toward darkness.
And keep looking to Christ.
Not once as a religious moment you remember from childhood.
Day after day.
When shame says, “Hide”...
look to Christ.
When pride says, “You don't need mercy”...
look to Christ.
When temptation says, “One more time”...
look to Christ.
When Satan whispers, “After what you did, God could never want you”...
look to Christ.
When self-righteousness whispers, “At least you're better than them”...
look to Christ.
The Cross destroys both despair and boasting.
Nobody standing beneath Calvary can truthfully say, “My sin wasn't serious.”
And nobody trusting the crucified and risen Christ needs to say, “My sin is stronger than His grace.”
This is why this message needs to travel beyond the people who already agree with it.
Not as superstition.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Not because sharing a post proves that you are a faithful Christian.
Religious.
Respected.
Confused.
Searching in the dark.
And perhaps this is the conversation that finally makes him look toward Jesus.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only a collection of religious rules.
Let them encounter Christ.

It is not an act that earns God's favor, and we will never pretend that it is. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him; supporting Gospel work can be one voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in making biblical truth available to others.
You need Jesus.
Not our merchandise.
Not our page.
Not our name.
Jesus.
The same Christ who spoke to Nicodemus in the darkness still calls people out of darkness today.
And perhaps that is the detail we have been reading past.
The story of the bronze serpent was never ultimately about becoming fascinated with a serpent.
It was about learning where a dying person must look.
Nicodemus came to Jesus at night.
Years later, after Jesus had been lifted up and crucified, John tells us that Nicodemus came with Joseph of Arimathea to care for His body.
The man who once approached Jesus beneath the cover of darkness was there when the lifted-up Savior was taken down from the Cross.
Imagine what he must have remembered.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness...”
Now he had seen it.
Not bronze.
Not a wilderness pole.
Jesus.
Lifted up.
The words from that nighttime conversation were no longer abstract theology.
There was blood on the body Nicodemus helped carry.
And maybe that is where this article needs to leave you.
Not staring at Nicodemus.
Not staring at Moses.
Not staring at the serpent.
Not staring at Gospel Warrior.
Not even staring endlessly at your own sin.
Look higher.
There is a Cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is a Savior.
There is mercy for the guilty.
There is cleansing for the stained.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is life for the dying.
There is grace for the scandal.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Talk to God.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Trust the One who was lifted up.
And if Christ has already rescued you, carry this Gospel toward somebody who is still dying from the poison.
Because somewhere tonight, another Nicodemus is still walking through the darkness.
And somewhere tonight, another wounded soul is still staring at the poison...
when God is calling them to look toward the Savior.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the Cross—but grace decides who you can become after you look to Jesus.
